content.text:
Pushed to [PR #29](https://github.com/hasToggle/memorynine/pull/29).

## What changed

**Erasure section** — "In Germany that is a legal right" → **"Anywhere in the EU that is a legal right."** I also put the article number back in the eyebrow: *The awkward request · GDPR Art. 17*. The emotional hook stays first; the legal anchor is right there for whoever forwards this to their DPO.

**Hero microcopy** — "German and English" → **"German, English, or whatever your client speaks."** The assistant answers in the language it was asked in, so the old line was narrowing the audience for no reason.

**The data FAQ** now answers instead of deferring:

> **The EU.** Recordings, transcripts and the knowledge base all sit in EU regions, and the transcription service only ever receives a link that expires. Money and health details are stripped out before anything else reads them, and every read is scoped to your workspace. The language models we call retain nothing and train on nothing — though a request can fail over to a provider outside the EU when one goes down, under those same terms. [The full picture, subprocessors included](/legal/privacy).

## On the level of transparency

You asked the right question, so let me give you my reasoning rather than just the output.

I put the failover caveat on the page. One clause, sequenced after the three strong claims and bundled with its mitigation. Three reasons:

1. **It's cheap here and expensive later.** This page's buyer forwards the data answer to legal. If "everything is in the EU" turns out to have an asterisk, it surfaces during procurement — the single worst moment, when you've already spent the sales cycle.
2. **The brand can't afford it.** Three sections up, the page says the product "won't sound sure" and "won't pass a rumour off as a fact." A privacy claim with a hidden asterisk refutes that argument on the same page. Precision *is* the positioning.
3. **Placed correctly, it reads as confidence.** Vague vendors say "enterprise-grade security." Naming the one edge and its mitigation in the same sentence reads like someone who knows their own system.

What I deliberately kept **off** the page: provider names, the Vercel AI Gateway, Atlas reranking running on GCP in the US, DPA mechanics, transfer bases. That's privacy-notice and ToS material — a landing page that lists subprocessors is arguing with itself.

If you'd rather the landing page just said "The EU" and left everything else to the privacy notice, it's a one-sentence deletion and I'll do it — but I'd advise against it.

## One thing that now needs your attention

The FAQ links to `/legal/privacy`, and that page is still fork boilerplate — it opens *"This Privacy Policy describes how has-toggle…"* with generic account/usage-data sections and no mention of transcription, model providers, EU regions, retention, or the erasure cascade. I've now pointed a compliance-minded reader straight at it.

Want me to write the privacy notice and ToS against what the code actually does? That's where the full detail you described belongs, and it's a well-scoped next task.

4	 *

7	 * `brand/mark.ts`, `brand/wordmark.ts` and `brand/lockup.ts` are the sources of
8	 * truth. Everything this writes is generated, including the SVGs under `brand/`
9	 * — committed so the logo can be opened in a design tool, or handed to someone
10	 * who asked for "the logo", without running anything.
11	 */
12	
13	import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
14	import { dirname, join } from "node:path";
15	import sharp from "sharp";
16	import { LOCKUP_HEIGHT, LOCKUP_WIDTH, lockupSvg } from "../brand/lockup";
17	import { INK, markSvg } from "../brand/mark";
18	import { wordmarkSvg } from "../brand/wordmark";
19	
20	/** The mark's own viewBox, and the density sharp rasterises it at 1:1. */
21	const MARK_SIZE = 32;
22	const BASE_DENSITY = 72;
23	
24	/**
25	 * The width the lockup is placed at in the transactional emails. The PNG is
26	 * rendered at twice that so it stays sharp on a retina screen.
27	 */
28	const EMAIL_LOCKUP_WIDTH = 160;
29	
30	const repoRoot = join(import.meta.dirname, "..", "..", "..");
31	
32	/**
33	 * sharp rasterises SVG at a DPI rather than a pixel size, so the density has to
34	 * be scaled to the target — otherwise the bitmap is an upscale of a 32px render.
35	 */
36	const rasterise = (svg: string, sourceWidth: number, targetWidth: number) =>
37	  sharp(Buffer.from(svg), {
38	    density: (BASE_DENSITY * targetWidth) / sourceWidth,
39	  });
40	
41	const markPng = (size: number, { rounded }: { rounded: boolean }) =>
42	  rasterise(markSvg({ rounded }), MARK_SIZE, size)
43	    .resize(size, size)
44	    .png()
45	    .toBuffer();
46	
47	/**
48	 * The lockup for email, where SVG is not a safe bet in any client. Flattened
49	 * onto white rather than left transparent: the clients that force their own
50	 * background turn a transparent PNG into a smear.
51	 */
52	const lockupPng = (width: number) =>
53	  rasterise(lockupSvg(), LOCKUP_WIDTH, width)
54	    .resize(width, Math.round((width * LOCKUP_HEIGHT) / LOCKUP_WIDTH))
55	    .flatten({ background: "#ffffff" })
56	    .png()
57	    .toBuffer();
58	
59	/**
60	 * A minimal ICO container: a 6-byte header, one 16-byte directory entry per
61	 * size, then the PNG payloads. PNG-in-ICO is understood by every browser that
62	 * still asks for `/favicon.ico`, so there is no BMP path to write.
63	 */
64	const ico = async (sizes: number[]) => {
65	  const images = await Promise.all(
66	    sizes.map((size) => markPng(size, { rounded: true }))
67	  );
68	
69	  const header = Buffer.alloc(6);
70	  header.writeUInt16LE(0, 0); // reserved
71	  header.writeUInt16LE(1, 2); // type: icon
72	  header.writeUInt16LE(images.length, 4);
73	
74	  const directorySize = 16 * images.length;
75	  let offset = header.length + directorySize;
76	
77	  const entries = images.map((image, index) => {
78	    const entry = Buffer.alloc(16);
79	    entry.writeUInt8(sizes[index] % 256, 0); // 256 is encoded as 0
80	    entry.writeUInt8(sizes[index] % 256, 1);
81	    entry.writeUInt8(0, 2); // palette size: none
82	    entry.writeUInt8(0, 3); // reserved
83	    entry.writeUInt16LE(1, 4); // colour planes
84	    entry.writeUInt16LE(32, 6); // bits per pixel
85	    entry.writeUInt32LE(image.length, 8);
86	    entry.writeUInt32LE(offset, 12);
87	    offset += image.length;
88	    return entry;
89	  });
90	
91	  return Buffer.concat([header, ...entries, ...images]);
92	};
93

96	  await mkdir(dirname(target), { recursive: true });

99	};

content.thinking:
I need to rethink the eyebrow label for the GDPR section — the user's right that calling it "awkward" misframes the customer's legitimate request as an inconvenience to the vendor. I'm considering alternatives like "When they ask to be forgotten," "The request you have to say yes to," or referencing the specific GDPR article directly, since the point is this is a non-negotiable legal obligation, not an awkward favor. I'm settling on "Erasure · GDPR Art. 17" as the eyebrow — it's factual and respectful without editorializing about the requester. The heading and closing line will carry the real value proposition. Let me make sure the body copy stays neutral too, keeping the focus on what the product does rather than how the request feels.

Now I need to write the privacy notice and terms of service. This is substantial legal work, so I'm being careful to ground everything in what the actual stack does, and I'll make clear these are drafts requiring a lawyer's review for GDPR compliance and German legal requirements. I won't invent legal entity details or addresses — I'll use placeholders instead. First, let me map out the actual tech stack and subprocessors from the codebase.

The stack includes Vercel for hosting and serverless functions, MongoDB Atlas for two databases handling auth and content, better-auth for self-hosted authentication, AssemblyAI for transcription, Vercel AI Gateway for LLM access, Voyage AI for reranking, Vercel Blob for private file storage with presigned URLs, Resend for email delivery, and Google Analytics plus PostHog for analytics tracking.

Rounding out the infrastructure are Sentry and BetterStack for observability, Arcjet for security, Stripe for payments (though it's unclear if payments are fully live given the "conversation" pricing model), Liveblocks for real-time collaboration, Knock for notifications, Vercel feature flags, and what looks like a CMS integration that's cut off.

I should verify which of these are actually wired up by checking the package configurations rather than assuming. On the data side, I'm seeing voice recordings, transcripts, forwarded emails, and extracted contact information from customers—that last one being particularly significant for data processing purposes.

The critical legal distinction here is that memorynine acts as a processor for workspace data (client knowledge) on behalf of the customer as controller, while being a controller itself for website visitors, marketing subscribers, and account administration. This controller-processor split is easy to get wrong but essential to document correctly.

I'll grep through the actual packages to confirm what's implemented, then write out the privacy policy and related legal documents.

---
title: "Privacy Notice"
description: "What memorynine does with data, where it sits, and who is responsible for what."
---

Last updated: 8 August 2026.

## The short version

memorynine records what your team says after a client call, turns it into a
memory the team can question, and shows you where every answer came from.

- **Your workspace content is yours.** Recordings, transcripts, forwarded mail
  and the facts drawn out of them belong to your company. We hold them on your
  instructions and for no other purpose.
- **Where it lives.** Recordings, transcripts and the knowledge base sit in EU
  regions. Speech-to-text runs on an EU endpoint.
- **Where it does not always live.** Language-model inference is routed through
  a gateway that fails over between providers, so an individual request can be
  processed outside the EU. Those providers retain nothing and train on nothing.
  [Details below](#where-data-is-processed).
- **What never reaches us.** Bank details, card numbers, passport and licence
  numbers, health conditions, medication and injuries are removed during
  transcription, before anything is stored.
- **We do not train models on your content.** Neither do the providers we call.
- **Erasing a person is real.** One action removes their facts, redacts them
  out of the transcripts and the review history, and marks their recordings for
  deletion. It cannot be undone.

The rest of this page is the detail behind those points.

## Who we are

**TO BE COMPLETED BEFORE PUBLISHING — the entries in this section are the only
placeholders in this document.**

- Controller within the meaning of Art. 4(7) GDPR: **[legal entity name and
  legal form]**
- Address: **[registered address]**
- Register and number: **[commercial register, HRB number]**
- Represented by: **[managing director]**
- Privacy contact: **[privacy@…]**
- Data protection officer: **[name and contact, or the sentence "We are not
  required to appoint one under Art. 37 GDPR and have not appointed one."]**

## Two different roles

Which rules apply depends on whose data it is. We are in one of two positions,
and the difference matters for your rights and for ours.

| What                                                                              | Our role      | Who decides what happens to it |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Visitors to this website                                                          | **Controller** | Us                             |
| People who ask for early access or a walkthrough                                  | **Controller** | Us                             |
| Account holders — your name, email, which workspace you belong to                 | **Controller** | Us                             |
| Billing records                                                                   | **Controller** | Us                             |
| Everything inside a workspace — recordings, transcripts, forwarded mail, the people and companies they describe, the facts drawn out of them | **Processor** | Your company                   |

That last row is most of the product. Your company decides what goes in, what
is confirmed, what is corrected and what is deleted. We process it on your
instructions under a data processing agreement (Art. 28 GDPR) and for nothing
else. If you are one of our customers' clients and want to know what is held
about you, the company you deal with is the right place to ask — and we help
them answer.

## What we process as controller

### When you visit this site

We process the request data your browser sends: IP address, user agent,
referring page, and the page you asked for. This is needed to serve the site
and to keep it standing up against abuse. Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, our
legitimate interest in operating and defending a website.

Product analytics run only with your consent, and the site works without them.
See [Cookies and analytics](#cookies-and-analytics).

### When you ask for early access

The form takes your email address. Before we store it, the address is checked
for format, against a list of disposable-mail domains, and against a
deliverability service — so the confirmation mail actually arrives and the list
is not used to bounce traffic at somebody else. We then send you a link, and
nothing else happens until you click it.

We keep your address, the confirmation status, and the timestamps. Legal basis:
Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR (your consent, given by confirming), and Art. 6(1)(f) for the
validity check. You can withdraw at any time by replying to any message from us
or writing to the privacy contact above; we delete the address.

### When you hold an account

better-auth stores your name, email address, a hashed password, your email
verification state, your sessions, which organisations you belong to and your
role in them, and any invitations you sent or received. Legal basis:
Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR — performing the contract you signed up for.

### Operating the service

We record one row per model call — which operation, how many tokens, what it
cost, and an identifier linking it to the source that triggered it. These rows
carry no content from your workspace. They exist for billing and for spotting a
worker that has started burning money. Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) and (f).

## What we process as processor

Everything below is workspace content. Your company is the controller; we act
on its instructions.

### Sources

- **Voice memos.** The audio file, its duration and content type, who recorded
  it, and when. Audio goes into private storage: it is not publicly reachable,
  and every read requires a signed link that expires.
- **Notes.** Whatever somebody typed or pasted.
- **Forwarded email.** The body, the original sender, who forwarded it, the
  subject, the message id and the date it was sent. Only addresses on your
  workspace's allowlist can post mail into it.
- **Transcripts.** The text produced from a voice memo, plus the detected
  language.

### What is removed before storage

Speech-to-text is instructed to redact these categories at the provider, so
they never reach our database at all:

account numbers, banking information, blood type, credit card number, expiry
and CVV, driver's licence numbers, drugs and medication, healthcare numbers,
injuries, medical conditions, medical procedures, passport numbers, and social
security numbers.

Names, companies and money amounts deliberately remain. They are the signal the
product exists to keep. If your team needs a category kept out that is not on
this list, tell us — the list is configuration, not architecture.

### Entities and facts

From a source, the extraction step drafts:

- **People** — name, email addresses, role, which organisation they belong to.
- **Organisations** — name, domains, industry, whether they are a lead, active
  or former.
- **Engagements** — title, type, status, start and end dates.
- **Facts** — a sentence about one of the above, its category, a confidence
  score, when it became true and when it stopped, and the source it came from.

Nothing in that list becomes part of the knowledge base until a person in your
workspace confirms it. Until then it sits as a draft in the review queue.

### The review trail

We keep who confirmed, edited or discarded each draft, and when. Without it
there is no way to answer "who decided this was true", which is the question
that makes the rest of the record worth anything.

## Where data is processed

| Component                                | Where                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Application, functions, static hosting   | EU regions                                                        |
| Database (accounts and knowledge base)   | EU region                                                         |
| Audio and attachment storage             | EU region, private, signed access only                            |
| Speech-to-text                           | EU endpoint                                                       |
| Language-model inference                 | Routed via a gateway; the serving region is not guaranteed        |
| Reranking of search results              | Processed outside the EU                                          |

The last two rows are the honest caveat, and we would rather you read it here
than discover it in a procurement review.

**Language-model inference.** Extraction, consolidation, contradiction checks
and answering your questions all call a language model through Vercel AI
Gateway. The gateway routes to whichever provider is healthy, which means an
individual request can be served outside the EU. Every provider we route to
operates under zero data retention: the request is processed and nothing is
kept, and nothing is used for training. What is sent is the text needed for
that one call — a transcript to be extracted from, or the facts relevant to a
question — never your whole knowledge base.

**Reranking.** When a question is asked, candidate facts are re-scored by a
cross-encoder that runs outside the EU. What is sent is the question and the
candidate fact texts. Nothing is retained.

Transfers outside the EU rest on the European Commission's standard
contractual clauses together with the transfer mechanisms our providers
maintain, and on Art. 46 GDPR. If your organisation cannot accept
model inference leaving the EU, say so before you start — it is a
configuration question, not a fixed property of the product, and we would
rather have that conversation up front.

## Subprocessors

These are the processors we use. We tell customers before adding one that
touches workspace content.

| Provider                          | What it does                                             | Touches workspace content |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Vercel                            | Hosting, serverless functions, private blob storage       | Yes                       |
| Vercel AI Gateway + model providers | Extraction, consolidation, contradiction checks, answers | Yes                       |
| MongoDB Atlas                     | Database                                                  | Yes                       |
| AssemblyAI                        | Speech-to-text, PII redaction                             | Yes                       |
| Voyage AI                         | Reranking search results                                  | Yes                       |
| Resend                            | Transactional email and the early-access list             | No                        |
| Sentry                            | Error tracking                                            | Incidentally, via errors  |
| BetterStack                       | Application logs                                          | Incidentally, via logs    |
| PostHog                           | Product analytics, with consent                           | No                        |
| Google Analytics                  | Website analytics, with consent                           | No                        |
| Arcjet                            | Bot and abuse protection                                  | No                        |
| Upstash                           | Rate limiting                                             | No                        |
| Knock                             | In-app notifications                                      | No                        |
| Liveblocks                        | Real-time presence                                        | No                        |
| Stripe                            | Payments, once billing starts                             | No                        |
| Abstract API                      | Email deliverability check on the early-access form       | No                        |
| BaseHub                           | Content for this site's blog and legal pages              | No                        |

"Incidentally" means we do not send content there on purpose, but an error
report or a log line can carry a fragment of whatever was being handled when
something broke. We keep identifiers out of logs where we can.

## How long we keep things

| What                                    | How long                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Workspace content                       | Until your company deletes it, or 30 days after the contract ends             |
| A person you erase                      | Removed immediately; see [Erasure](#erasure)                                  |
| Account and session data                | For as long as the account exists, then deleted                               |
| Early-access address                    | Until you withdraw, or 24 months after the last contact                       |
| Unconfirmed early-access address        | The confirmation link expires after 24 hours; unconfirmed entries are cleared |
| Usage and cost records                  | Kept as billing history                                                       |
| Error reports and logs                  | As configured at the provider, currently short-term                           |
| Records we must keep by law             | For the statutory period, commercial and tax law included                     |

## Erasure

When somebody exercises their right under Art. 17 GDPR, your workspace can
erase them in one action. That does the following, and we mention it here
because "we will delete your data" usually means less than people assume:

- Every fact anchored to that person is deleted, including facts that were
  consolidated out of them, which an anchor-scoped delete would otherwise miss.
- Facts about other people that still mention them by name are redacted.
- Their name and addresses are removed from the source transcripts and from the
  review history, so the record that a meeting happened survives without them
  in it.
- Recordings and attachments that no longer back any surviving fact are marked
  for deletion, and the stored files go with them.
- Derived caches built from any of the above are dropped and rebuilt.

It is irreversible. There is no recycle bin, because a recycle bin would mean
we kept a copy.

## Your rights

Under the GDPR you can ask for access to your data (Art. 15), correction
(Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), a portable copy
(Art. 20), and you can object to processing based on legitimate interests
(Art. 21). Where processing rests on consent, you can withdraw it at any time,
without affecting what was lawful before you did.

Write to the privacy contact above. We answer within one month.

**One routing note.** For anything inside a customer's workspace, that customer
is the controller, not us. If you are a client of a company that uses
memorynine, ask them — they can see the record, they can correct it, and they
can erase you. If you approach us instead, we will pass the request on and tell
you we have.

## Automated decision-making

There is none within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR. The assistant drafts and
proposes; a person confirms. Nothing it produces has a legal or similarly
significant effect on anyone by itself, and nothing enters the knowledge base
without a human saying so.

The assistant can be wrong, and it is built to say when it does not know rather
than fill the gap. Answers carry the source they rest on so a reader can check
them. That is a design decision, not a legal guarantee: what your team repeats
to a client is your team's responsibility.

## Cookies and analytics

Strictly necessary cookies — your session, your consent choice — are set
without asking, because the site does not work without them. Everything else
waits for your consent, and you can withdraw it at any time. Legal basis for
non-essential cookies and similar technologies: Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR together with
§ 25(1) TDDDG.

## Security

Access to a workspace is scoped on every single read, from the signed-in
session rather than from anything a user or a model can influence — so there is
no question that reaches another workspace's data. Recordings sit in private
storage reachable only through links that expire. Passwords are hashed.
Transport is encrypted. Material arriving from outside — a forwarded thread, a
transcript — is treated as text somebody wrote, never as an instruction to the
assistant.

## Complaints

If you think we have handled your data badly, tell us first — we would rather
fix it. You can also complain to a supervisory authority, in the member state
where you live, work, or where the problem happened.

## Changes

We update this notice when the product changes. The date at the top is when it
last changed. If a change affects workspace content or adds a subprocessor that
touches it, we tell customers rather than relying on you to re-read this page.

| Database (accounts and knowledge base)   | EU region                                                         |

| Speech-to-text                           | EU endpoint                                                       |
| Language-model inference                 | Routed via a gateway; the serving region is not guaranteed        |
| Reranking of search results              | Processed outside the EU                                          |

The last two rows are the honest caveat, and we would rather you read it here
than discover it in a procurement review.

**Language-model inference.** Extraction, consolidation, contradiction checks
and answering your questions all call a language model through Vercel AI
Gateway. The gateway routes to whichever provider is healthy, which means an
individual request can be served outside the EU. Every provider we route to
operates under zero data retention: the request is processed and nothing is
kept, and nothing is used for training. What is sent is the text needed for
that one call — a transcript to be extracted from, or the facts relevant to a
question — never your whole knowledge base.

**Reranking.** When a question is asked, candidate facts are re-scored by a
cross-encoder that runs outside the EU. What is sent is the question and the
candidate fact texts. Nothing is retained.

Transfers outside the EU rest on the European Commission's standard
contractual clauses together with the transfer mechanisms our providers
maintain, and on Art. 46 GDPR. If your organisation cannot accept
model inference leaving the EU, say so before you start — it is a
configuration question, not a fixed property of the product, and we would
rather have that conversation up front.

These are the processors we use. We tell customers before adding one that
touches workspace content.

| Provider                          | What it does                                             | Touches workspace content |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Vercel                            | Hosting, serverless functions, private blob storage       | Yes                       |
| Vercel AI Gateway + model providers | Extraction, consolidation, contradiction checks, answers | Yes                       |
| MongoDB Atlas                     | Database                                                  | Yes                       |
| AssemblyAI                        | Speech-to-text, PII redaction                             | Yes                       |
| Voyage AI                         | Reranking search results                                  | Yes                       |
| Resend                            | Transactional email and the early-access list             | No                        |
| Sentry                            | Error tracking                                            | Incidentally, via errors  |
| BetterStack                       | Application logs                                          | Incidentally, via logs    |
| PostHog                           | Product analytics, with consent                           | No                        |
| Google Analytics                  | Website analytics, with consent                           | No                        |
| Arcjet                            | Bot and abuse protection                                  | No                        |
| Upstash                           | Rate limiting                                             | No                        |
| Knock                             | In-app notifications                                      | No                        |
| Liveblocks                        | Real-time presence                                        | No                        |
| Stripe                            | Payments, once billing starts                             | No                        |
| Abstract API                      | Email deliverability check on the early-access form       | No                        |
| BaseHub                           | Content for this site's blog and legal pages              | No                        |

"Incidentally" means we do not send content there on purpose, but an error
report or a log line can carry a fragment of whatever was being handled when
something broke. We keep identifiers out of logs where we can.

## How long we keep things

| What                                    | How long                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Workspace content                       | Until your company deletes it, or 30 days after the contract ends             |
| A person you erase                      | Removed immediately; see [Erasure](#erasure)                                  |
| Account and session data                | For as long as the account exists, then deleted                               |
| Early-access address                    | Until you withdraw, or 24 months after the last contact                       |
| Unconfirmed early-access address        | The confirmation link expires after 24 hours; unconfirmed entries are cleared |
| Usage and cost records                  | Kept as billing history                                                       |
| Error reports and logs                  | As configured at the provider, currently short-term                           |
| Records we must keep by law             | For the statutory period, commercial and tax law included                     |

## Erasure

When somebody exercises their right under Art. 17 GDPR, your workspace can
erase them in one action. That does the following, and we mention it here
because "we will delete your data" usually means less than people assume:

- Every fact anchored to that person is deleted, including facts that were
  consolidated out of them, which an anchor-scoped delete would otherwise miss.
- Facts about other people that still mention them by name are redacted.
- Their name and addresses are removed from the source transcripts and from the
  review history, so the record that a meeting happened survives without them
  in it.
- Recordings and attachments that no longer back any surviving fact are marked
  for deletion, and the stored files go with them.
- Derived caches built from any of the above are dropped and rebuilt.

It is irreversible. There is no recycle bin, because a recycle bin would mean
we kept a copy.

## Your rights

Under the GDPR you can ask for access to your data (Art. 15), correction
(Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), a portable copy
(Art. 20), and you can object to processing based on legitimate interests
(Art. 21). Where processing rests on consent, you can withdraw it at any time,
without affecting what was lawful before you did.

Write to the privacy contact above. We answer within one month.

**One routing note.** For anything inside a customer's workspace, that customer
is the controller, not us. If you are a client of a company that uses
memorynine, ask them — they can see the record, they can correct it, and they
can erase you. If you approach us instead, we will pass the request on and tell
you we have.

## Automated decision-making

There is none within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR. The assistant drafts and
proposes; a person confirms. Nothing it produces has a legal or similarly
significant effect on anyone by itself, and nothing enters the knowledge base
without a human saying so.

The assistant can be wrong, and it is built to say when it does not know rather
than fill the gap. Answers carry the source they rest on so a reader can check
them. That is a design decision, not a legal guarantee: what your team repeats
to a client is your team's responsibility.

## Cookies and analytics

Strictly necessary cookies — your session, your consent choice — are set
without asking, because the site does not work without them. Everything else
waits for your consent, and you can withdraw it at any time. Legal basis for
non-essential cookies and similar technologies: Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR together with
§ 25(1) TDDDG.

## Security

Access to a workspace is scoped on every single read, from the signed-in
session rather than from anything a user or a model can influence — so there is
no question that reaches another workspace's data. Recordings sit in private
storage reachable only through links that expire. Passwords are hashed.
Transport is encrypted. Material arriving from outside — a forwarded thread, a
transcript — is treated as text somebody wrote, never as an instruction to the
assistant.

## Complaints

If you think we have handled your data badly, tell us first — we would rather
fix it. You can also complain to a supervisory authority, in the member state
where you live, work, or where the problem happened.

## Changes

We update this notice when the product changes. The date at the top is when it
last changed. If a change affects workspace content or adds a subprocessor that
touches it, we tell customers rather than relying on you to re-read this page.

---
title: "Terms of Service"
description: "What we owe you, what you owe us, and the parts of this that are your call to make."
---

Last updated: 8 August 2026.

These terms are written to be read. Where a sentence could be shorter without
losing its meaning, it is. Where it is long, that is because the detail matters.

## 1. Who this is between

These terms are the agreement between **[legal entity name — see the
[privacy notice](/legal/privacy) for the details still to be completed]** ("we",
"us") and the company that opens a workspace ("you", "your company").

memorynine is sold to businesses. By opening a workspace you confirm you are
acting in the course of a trade, business or profession within the meaning of
§ 14 BGB, and not as a consumer. If you are a consumer, these terms are not for
you and you should not sign up.

## 2. What the service does

memorynine takes what your team captures after client conversations — voice
memos, typed notes, forwarded email — transcribes and reads it, drafts the
people, companies, engagements and facts it finds, and puts those drafts in
front of one of your people to confirm or discard. What gets confirmed becomes
a knowledge base your team can question in plain language, with each answer
showing the material it rests on.

## 3. Early access

The service is early. That has consequences, and they are not buried in a
clause at the bottom:

- Features change, and some will be removed.
- We do not promise a service level yet. There is no uptime guarantee and no
  support response time.
- We may contact you about how you are using it, because that is how it gets
  better.

We will not, however, make a change that loses your data without telling you
first and giving you a way to take it with you.

## 4. Accounts and workspaces

You are responsible for who you let into your workspace and for what they do
there. Keep credentials to yourself, do not share logins, and tell us promptly
if you think an account has been compromised.

Each workspace sees only its own data. That is enforced on every read, from the
signed-in session — not from anything a user or a model can influence.

## 5. Recording is your call, and your responsibility

This is the most important clause in this document, so it is not at the bottom.

memorynine is designed around a memo you record **about** a conversation, after
it, in your own voice. That is a different thing from recording the
conversation itself, and the law treats it very differently.

- In Germany, recording somebody's spoken word without their consent can be a
  criminal offence under § 201 StGB. It is not a grey area, and it does not
  become one because the recording was useful.
- Elsewhere in the EU the rules differ by member state, and some require every
  participant's consent.
- Whether you may capture what a client told you, and whether you must tell
  them you are doing it, is a question about your relationship with them. It is
  not a question we can answer for you.

So: **you decide what goes into your workspace, and you carry the legal
responsibility for it.** You confirm that you have a lawful basis for the
personal data you put in, that you have met your information duties under
Art. 13 and 14 GDPR toward the people it describes, and that you are not
uploading recordings you had no right to make.

We will not police this for you, and we would be doing you a disservice if we
implied that using our product settled it.

## 6. Data protection

For everything inside your workspace, your company is the controller and we are
the processor. We process it on your documented instructions and for no other
purpose. A data processing agreement under Art. 28 GDPR is part of this
contract; ask and we will send it before you put real client data in.

The [privacy notice](/legal/privacy) sets out where data sits, which
subprocessors are involved, what is redacted before storage, and what erasing a
person actually does. It is part of these terms by reference.

Do not deliberately put special categories of data (Art. 9 GDPR) into a
workspace — health, beliefs, union membership, and the rest. The transcription
step strips the medical and financial categories it can recognise, but that is
data minimisation, not a filter you should rely on.

## 7. What you may not do

- Break the law with it, or help somebody else to.
- Put in material you have no right to hold.
- Try to reach another workspace's data, or test whether you can without
  telling us first. If you are a security researcher, write to us; we will
  answer properly.
- Resell the service, or use it to build a competing one.
- Automate access in a way that degrades it for everybody else.

## 8. What the assistant says is not advice

The assistant drafts, cites and answers. It does not decide.

It is built to say when it does not know, to show both sides of a
contradiction, and to mark material nobody has confirmed. Those are real
design commitments and they are tested. They are not a warranty that any given
answer is correct.

Every answer carries the material it rests on precisely so a person can check
it. What your team repeats to a client is your team's word, not ours.

## 9. Your content stays yours

You keep every right you had in what you put in, and in what comes out of it.
We claim no ownership over your workspace and no licence beyond what running
the service requires — storing it, processing it, showing it back to you, and
keeping backups.

We do not use your workspace content to train models, and the providers we call
operate under zero data retention. If we ever want to learn something from
aggregate, non-identifying usage patterns, we will ask first.

## 10. What we own

The software, the interface, the design and the name are ours. Nothing here
transfers any of it to you.

## 11. Fees

Pricing is agreed with you directly while we are setting up the first
workspaces. Whatever we agree is what applies; if that changes we tell you at
least 30 days ahead, and you may end the contract before the new price starts.

## 12. Ending it

You can stop at any time, and so can we, with 30 days' notice. Either of us can
end it immediately for a serious breach that is not fixed within 14 days of
being pointed out.

When it ends:

- You can export your workspace for 30 days.
- After that we delete it, including backups on their normal cycle.
- We keep what the law requires us to keep, and nothing else.

## 13. Availability

We aim to keep it up and we will tell you about planned downtime. During early
access there is no guaranteed availability. Some of what the product depends on
— speech-to-text, model inference — sits with providers we do not control, and
when one of them is down, part of the pipeline waits. Captured material is not
lost when that happens; it is picked up when the provider returns.

## 14. Liability

We are liable without limit for injury to life, body or health, for intent and
gross negligence, under the Produkthaftungsgesetz, and where we have given a
guarantee.

For simple negligence we are liable only where we breach an obligation that is
essential to this contract and that you were entitled to rely on — and then
only for the foreseeable damage typical of a contract like this one.

All other liability is excluded. This applies equally to our staff and to
anybody we engage.

## 15. Confidentiality

What you show us about your business while we set you up, and what we show you
about how the product works, stays between us. That obligation outlives the
contract.

## 16. Changes to these terms

We will tell you at least 30 days before a change takes effect. If you do not
accept it, end the contract before it starts. Continuing to use the service
after that date means you accept the new version.

## 17. Law and venue

German law applies, and the UN Convention on Contracts for the International
Sale of Goods does not.

Place of jurisdiction is our registered seat, provided you are a merchant, a
legal person under public law, or a special fund under public law.

If any clause here turns out to be invalid, the rest stays in force.

## 18. Getting in touch

Write to the address in the [privacy notice](/legal/privacy). A real person
answers.

content.text:
Pushed to [PR #29](https://github.com/hasToggle/memorynine/pull/29).

## The eyebrow

You're right, and the reason it grated is worth naming: "awkward" put the discomfort on the person exercising a right they're entitled to. It's not awkward for them — it's a two-week scramble for *you*, which is the thing the section actually sells against. It now reads **Erasure · GDPR Art. 17** — plain, factual, and the heading (*"Please delete everything you have on me."*) carries the emotion without editorialising about whoever said it.

## Privacy notice and terms

Both written from the code, not a template.

**The structural decision** in the privacy notice is the one most vendor notices blur: we're **controller** for the website, the early-access list and account admin — and **processor** for everything inside a workspace. That's most of the product. It means a data subject's request goes to *your customer*, not to us, so the notice says so and commits to helping them answer it. There's a table so nobody has to infer which row they're in.

Everything factual is drawn from the repo:

- **The redaction list** is the actual `DEFAULT_PII_POLICIES` array — bank details, card numbers, passport and licence numbers, health conditions, medication, injuries. With the line that names, companies and money amounts deliberately stay, because they're the signal.
- **Entity and fact fields** are the Zod schemas.
- **The erasure section** describes what `erasePerson` really does, including the consolidated facts an anchor-scoped delete would miss and the review-trail redaction.
- **Where data sits** gets its own section: EU for hosting, database, blob storage and speech-to-text (`api.eu.assemblyai.com`); gateway-routed inference that can be served outside the EU; reranking outside by design. Both under zero retention, stated plainly rather than buried.
- **The subprocessor table** is the integrations that exist in the repo, marked *Yes / Incidentally / No* for workspace content — Sentry and BetterStack get "incidentally," because an error report can carry a fragment of whatever broke.
- **Art. 22**: none. The assistant proposes, a person confirms.

**The terms** put recording consent in **section 5**, not the fine print. The product is built around a memo you record *about* a conversation, in your own voice — legally a different act from recording the conversation, and § 201 StGB isn't a grey area. That clause says the customer decides and the customer carries it, because implying our product settles the question would be a disservice. It's also B2B-only (§ 14 BGB), which keeps German AGB law on the right footing.

I also found the SEO `applicationName` was still `has-toggle`, so every page title said so. Fixed, and the two tests asserting the old brand updated.

## What you need to do before these go live

**Placeholders.** All of them sit in one block — "Who we are" in the privacy notice: legal entity and form, registered address, register/HRB number, managing director, privacy contact, and a DPO line (name, or the sentence saying you're not required to appoint one). They render in bold with a **TO BE COMPLETED BEFORE PUBLISHING** header, so they can't ship by accident. The terms reference that section rather than repeating it.

**Three things I flagged rather than guessed:**

1. **These are drafts written from the system, not legal advice.** A Rechtsanwalt should review before publishing — particularly the liability clause and the Art. 28 arrangement.
2. **There's no Impressum.** § 5 DDG requires one for a commercial German site, and the footer links only Privacy and Terms. I didn't scaffold it because a page of placeholders is worse than no page. Say the word once you have the entity details.
3. **No German version.** For a DACH-facing product this matters — both commercially and because the GDPR expects information in language the data subject actually understands. The legal MDX isn't locale-aware today (`getLegalPage(slug)` ignores locale), so that's a small routing change plus translation.

**One thing to verify:** the subprocessor table lists everything wired in the repo, but several keys are optional (Arcjet, Upstash, Knock, Liveblocks, Sentry, BetterStack, GA, Voyage, Stripe). Check which are actually enabled in production and prune the ones that aren't — listing a processor you don't use is sloppy in a different direction.

## Verified
`bun run check` clean · `turbo typecheck test` 30/30 · web builds · both legal pages rendered in the browser with tables, TOC and anchors working.

9

11	memory the team can question, and shows you where every answer came from.

20	  processed outside the EU. Those providers retain nothing and train on nothing.

67

69	
70	We process the request data your browser sends: IP address, user agent,
71	referring page, and the page you asked for. This is needed to serve the site
72	and to keep it standing up against abuse. Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, our
73	legitimate interest in operating and defending a website.
74	
75	Product analytics run only with your consent, and the site works without them.
76	See [Cookies and analytics](#cookies-and-analytics).
77	
78	### When you ask for early access
79

99

scaffolding that nothing ever mounted. No Room is rendered anywhere, and the two

resolveUsers and resolveMentionSuggestions callbacks, so nothing called them
either. getUsers would not even have typechecked without the global type that
liveblocks.config.ts declared.

Gone: the package, the config, the /api/collaboration/auth route, both user
actions, the env keys, the workspace dependency, fuse.js (there for the mention
search alone), and the Biome exclusion pointing at a file that no longer exists.
Removed from the privacy notice's subprocessor table and from CLAUDE.md.

Left alone: the two dated design specs under docs/superpowers that mention it.
